name: An e-shop with 60 employees has one IT administrator who also "does security", mostly backups and user accounts. After a data breach the CEO wants to take security seriously and asks you for options. a) Which typical company-size model does the e-shop match now, and what are its weaknesses? b) Compare two next steps – a small all-purpose security team, or specialised teams like a large company – with their pros and cons for this e-shop. c) Which security functions (sub-teams) would you prioritise first and why, and how would you avoid security becoming "minimal budget, minimal respect" again once the breach is forgotten?
answer:
a) It matches the small company: no security team, a one-man show inside IT, security seen as not very important and reduced to backup and authentication. Pro: at least one person who understands security. Con: everything depends on the knowledge and experience of one person; minimal budget, people and respect ("why should we be a target") – typical until a major incident or audit, which has just happened.
b) Small all-purpose team (medium-sized model): a dedicated security team covering operational, infrastructure and application layers; cons – limited budget and limited experience in all areas ("nobody knows everything"), risk of being seen as an unnecessary evil. Specialised teams (large company): detailed experience and possibly a dedicated budget, but security costs a lot and slows innovation – out of proportion for 60 employees. A small team is the realistic step.
c) Interpretation: first the functions that would have caught or limited the breach – monitoring and incident response (SOC tasks: correlating logs, alerts, an incident database, disaster recovery plans, possibly outsourced), and security architecture (policies, risk assessment, design review of changes); later application security / pentesting for the web shop. Keeping attention: regular reporting to management with security metrics/KPIs, change management with security review, a framework (CIS Controls IG1 or NIST CSF) to show progress, and compliance (internal audits) so that security does not depend on the memory of the incident.
keyPoints: Now the small-company model: one admin, backup and authentication; depends on one person
Security taken seriously mostly after an incident or audit; otherwise minimal budget and respect
Medium model: small all-purpose team – budget and experience limits
Large model: specialised teams and budget, but costly and slower innovation – disproportionate here
Priorities: monitoring and incident response (SOC tasks), architecture and risk assessment
Keep attention: KPIs and reporting, change management, frameworks, internal audits
source: Lecture 5, slides 2–12, 14–15, 20, 24, 40; the recommendation for the e-shop is an interpretation

name: Your organisation runs a popular network-monitoring product from an external vendor; it has wide privileges in your network and installs the vendor's signed updates automatically, as security guidelines recommend. Using the SolarWinds case as a precedent: a) explain how such a supply-chain attack works and why careful, well-patched customers were the ones hit; b) what the attacker's behaviour (target selection, dormancy, hiding) means for detecting it; c) propose security-operations measures that would limit or reveal such a compromise in your organisation.
answer:
a) In SolarWinds the attacker (UNC2452, revealed by FireEye) got into the vendor, first injected test code and then the SUNBURST malware into builds of Orion, a network-management product used by governments and large corporations and approved for sensitive areas. The malware was shipped as a regular update – so precisely the customers who carefully kept Orion patched and updated installed it (about 18,000 organisations). The trust in the supplier's update channel is the attack vector.
b) SUNBURST waited about 14 days, went live only at a handful of valuable targets and slept indefinitely elsewhere; the actor was very sophisticated – cleaned trace evidence, secured and hid its servers, hid the exploit; the motivation was murky (no financial interest, no ransomware, no data destruction, no DoS). Detection therefore cannot rely on visible damage or mass indicators – the activity is quiet and targeted.
c) (Derived from the SecOps processes in the lecture.) Least privilege and segmentation for the monitoring product (it should not reach everything); SOC monitoring – correlate network, server and security logs, alert on unusual outbound connections of management servers, maintain threat intelligence and an incident database; security design review and change management for new vendor tools (justification, network and user access control, logging); supplier management – contractual incident reporting and audit rights; frameworks – CIS Controls / NIST CSF Detect and Respond functions, MITRE ATT&CK to describe and hunt adversary techniques; disaster recovery plans in case the tool must be cut off.
keyPoints: SUNBURST in SolarWinds Orion updates – supply-chain attack via a trusted update channel
Careful, patched customers were hit precisely because they installed updates
Dormant ~14 days, activated only at a few valuable targets; very sophisticated hiding
Murky motivation: no financial interest, no ransomware, no data destruction
Detection must rely on monitoring and correlation, not visible damage
Measures: least privilege/segmentation for vendor tools, SOC monitoring, design review, supplier contracts, ATT&CK/CSF
source: Lecture 5, slides 8–15, 20–31, 35–39; lecture 3, slide 5; the measures in c) are derived
